**Lithium** (from [Ancient Greek](/wiki/Ancient_Greek_language "Ancient Greek language"): λίθος, *líthos*, 'stone') is a [chemical element](/wiki/Chemical_element "Chemical element"); it has [symbol](/wiki/Chemical_symbol "Chemical symbol") **Li** and [atomic number](/wiki/Atomic_number "Atomic number") 3. It is a soft, silvery-white [alkali metal](/wiki/Alkali_metal "Alkali metal"). Under [standard conditions](/wiki/Standard_temperature_and_pressure "Standard temperature and pressure"), it is the least dense metal and the least dense solid element. Like all alkali metals, lithium is highly [reactive](/wiki/Reactivity_(chemistry) "Reactivity (chemistry)") and flammable, and must be stored in vacuum, inert atmosphere, or inert liquid such as purified [kerosene](/wiki/Kerosene "Kerosene")[[7]](#cite_note-7) or mineral oil. It exhibits a metallic [luster](/wiki/Luster_(mineralogy) "Luster (mineralogy)") when pure, but quickly [corrodes](/wiki/Corrosion "Corrosion") in air to a dull silvery gray, then black tarnish. It does not occur freely in nature, but occurs mainly as [pegmatitic](/wiki/Pegmatite "Pegmatite") minerals, which were once the main source of lithium. Due to its solubility as an ion, it is present in ocean water and is commonly obtained from [brines](/wiki/Brine "Brine"). Lithium metal is isolated [electrolytically](/wiki/Electrolysis "Electrolysis") from a mixture of [lithium chloride](/wiki/Lithium_chloride "Lithium chloride") and [potassium chloride](/wiki/Potassium_chloride "Potassium chloride").
